messages.content: The internet is down at our house. Everything stopped working at once. Where do I even start?

Start with the one question that splits every home-network problem in half: is it ONE device, or EVERY device?

Pick up a second device — a phone, a tablet, anything — and try the same thing. If the phone works and only the living-room TV is dead, your internet is fine and the problem lives inside that one device or its connection to your router. If nothing in the house works, the problem is upstream of all of them: the router, the modem, or the line coming into the house.

This sounds too simple to matter, but it decides where you spend the next hour. People factory-reset routers over a TV that had quietly joined the wrong network, and they reinstall apps on phones while the modem sat dark. One minute with a second device tells you which half of the world to work in.

While you check, look at the modem (the box the cable or fiber line plugs into) and just note its lights — don't touch anything yet. A modem with its normal lights lit is telling a different story from a modem that's dark or blinking a pattern you've never seen. Write down what you see. That observation is evidence, and the next steps all build on it.
Support told me to restart everything, so I unplugged the modem and router and plugged them both back in at the same time. It still doesn't work. Does the order really matter?

It does, and here's the mechanism. Your modem has one job first: synchronize with the provider's network — lock onto the cable or fiber signal, register itself, and get assigned your connection. That takes anywhere from one to five minutes, and until it finishes, the modem has nothing to hand anyone.

Your router's job starts after that: it asks the modem for a public address and becomes the house's gateway. If the router boots while the modem is still synchronizing, the router asks too early, gets nothing, and on many models it gives up and sits there holding a bad or empty address until it's restarted again.

So: unplug both. Plug in the modem alone. Wait until its lights settle into their normal, steady pattern — the online/internet light solid, not cycling. Then plug in the router and give it two or three minutes. Then test.

Restarting in the wrong order is one of the most common reasons 'I already rebooted it three times' didn't fix anything. The equipment wasn't broken; it was woken up in the wrong sequence.
A friend said to plug my laptop straight into the modem to test. What does that actually prove, and is it different from plugging into the router?

It's the single most informative test you can run, because it removes half the equipment from the story. Do it in two steps.

First, plug the laptop into a LAN port on your router with an Ethernet cable and run a speed test. If that's fast and solid but Wi-Fi in the same room is miserable, the internet coming into the house is fine and your problem is the wireless leg — placement, interference, or a tired router radio.

Second, if wired-through-the-router is also bad, unplug the router, connect the laptop directly to the modem, and restart the modem so it learns the laptop is its new partner. Test again. Fast at the modem but slow through the router convicts the router. Slow even at the modem means the fault is the modem or the provider's line — their side of the line, their problem to fix.

Two cautions. While the laptop is plugged straight into the modem, it's exposed directly to the internet without your router's firewall in front of it — fine for a ten-minute test, not a way to live. And afterwards, reconnect the router and restart the modem again so it re-registers with the router.
My modem has a row of lights labeled Power, Downstream, Upstream, Online, and Link. The Downstream one has been blinking for twenty minutes. What is it telling me?

Those lights are a progress report on a conversation, read left to right. Power: the box is alive. Downstream blinking: the modem is listening for and trying to lock onto the provider's signal coming toward you. Downstream solid: locked. Upstream: the return path, your signal going out. Online solid: the modem has registered with the provider and been given your connection. Link: something is plugged into it and talking.

A Downstream light that blinks forever means the modem cannot find a usable signal on the line. That's rarely the modem's fault. It means the conversation never starts: a cut or damaged cable, a connector worked loose (check the coax is finger-tight at the wall and the modem), a failed splitter, or an outage on the provider's plant.

What you can do: reseat the cable connections, remove any splitter you can bypass for a test, and restart the modem once. If Downstream still won't lock, you've reached the demarcation line — the fault is on the provider's side or in the wiring feeding the modem, and the blinking light is exactly the evidence to report: 'Downstream won't sync since 7 pm' tells a technician more than 'the internet is broken.'
My phone says it's connected to Wi-Fi with full bars, but nothing loads and there's a little exclamation mark. How can Wi-Fi be 'connected' and the internet still be down?

Because those are two different connections wearing one icon. The Wi-Fi link is just the short radio hop between your phone and your router across the room. When your phone says 'connected,' it means that hop succeeded — it found the router, authenticated, and got a local address. Full bars measure only that hop.

The internet is the second leg: router to modem to provider. Your phone quietly tests that leg too, and the exclamation mark is its verdict: 'I'm talking to your router fine, but your router can't reach the internet.' Android often spells it out as 'Connected, no internet.'

So the icon has already done the great separation for you. Every device in the house will show the same symptom, because they all share the dead second leg. Don't troubleshoot the phone. Go look at the modem: if its Online light is out or cycling, restart in order — modem first, wait for sync, then router. If the modem claims to be online and the mark persists, restart just the router. The phone was never the patient; it was the messenger.
The kids' tablets work fine in the kitchen, but the TV in the back bedroom says no connection. Is my internet broken or not?

Your internet is almost certainly fine — and the working tablets just proved it. If the service coming into the house were down, the kitchen would be dead too. What you have is a local problem: one device, in one place.

Work the short list for that TV. First, distance and walls: the back bedroom is probably the farthest point from the router, with the most walls in between — the signal may simply arrive too weak, and TVs are notorious for having mediocre Wi-Fi radios tucked behind a big metal panel that blocks signal further. Second, check which network the TV is joined to: after a router restart or a software update, devices sometimes rejoin a guest network or an old extender name that no longer leads anywhere. Third, restart the TV itself — fully off at the wall for thirty seconds, since 'off' on a modern TV is usually just standby, and its network stack may have been awake and confused for months.

If the TV works when you temporarily move it (or when you stand near it with a phone and the phone also struggles), you've convicted the location, not the TV. That's a coverage problem, solved with placement or a wired run — not a call to your provider.
Every time it rains hard, our internet drops or crawls for a few hours, then fixes itself. My provider says they can't find anything when they check. What's going on?

That pattern is a classic signature, and the self-healing is exactly why the provider's checks miss it. Water is getting into something on the outside plant — a cracked cable jacket, a corroded connector in the pedestal box at the street, a damaged splice — and when rain fills it, the signal degrades. When it dries, the fault evaporates, and a technician testing on a sunny Tuesday finds a healthy line.

Everything outside your house, and the drop cable running to it, is the provider's side of the demarcation line. Don't open pedestals or climb anything; that's their equipment and their job. Your job is evidence, because intermittent weather faults are won with logs, not arguments.

Keep a simple record for two or three storms: date, time the drops started, time they cleared, what the modem lights did, and the weather. Note whether neighbors on the same provider lose service too — ask once, it matters. Then call and use the words that route the ticket correctly: 'intermittent sync loss correlated with rain, suspected water ingress in the outside plant.' Ask for the ticket number. A dated log converts 'we can't find anything' into a plant-maintenance job, because it tells the line crew when and where to look.
The internet died an hour ago. Should I reset my router to factory settings and set it up again from scratch?

No — and this is the moment when that instinct does real damage. Before you change anything, check whether the outage is yours at all. Open your provider's app or outage page on your phone using mobile data, or glance at a neighbor's house on the same service if you can. Area outages are common, and no amount of resetting fixes a cut line down the street.

A factory reset is the most destructive tool in the drawer. It erases your network name, passphrase, and every setting you've tuned, and if the real fault was upstream, you end the outage with a second, self-inflicted problem: reconfiguring everything while tired. It also destroys evidence — support can learn things from a router's current state that a blank one can't tell them.

The proportionate ladder is: look at the modem lights, restart modem then router in order, run one wired test. That's it for the first hour. Factory reset belongs at the very end of troubleshooting, when the equipment itself is convicted and there's nothing left to lose — not at the beginning, when the fault hasn't even been located yet.
All the lights on both boxes look completely normal, but no device in the house can get online. If the lights are happy, what could be wrong?

Lights report what each box believes about its own link, and a box can be sincerely wrong about the wider world. Two usual suspects hide behind normal lights.

First, the router's software has hung in a way that leaves the lights lit — it still advertises Wi-Fi and answers nothing. Second, the router lost or never properly got its public address from the modem during some earlier hiccup, so it cheerfully routes your traffic to nowhere.

Restart one box at a time so you learn something. Restart only the router first, wait three minutes, test. If service returns, the router's software was the fault — note the date; a router that needs this monthly is aging, and one that needs it weekly is telling you it's done. If the router restart changes nothing, restart the modem, let it fully sync, then restart the router once more so it takes a fresh address.

The one-at-a-time discipline matters: rebooting everything at once fixes the symptom and teaches you nothing, so the next occurrence starts from zero again. A two-line note — 'router-only restart fixed it, Oct 3' — turns the next outage into a thirty-second job.
We had a one-second power flicker. The modem came back but the router never did, and now it won't power on at all. Coincidence?

Probably not a coincidence. A flicker isn't a clean off-and-on; it's often a sag followed by a surge as power returns, and small power supplies — the wall-wart bricks that feed routers — are the frailest part of the whole setup. Yours may have died protecting, or failing to protect, the router. Test the cheap thing first: if you have another adapter with the same voltage, polarity, and at least the same current rating, try it. Routers that 'die' in flickers are very often just orphaned by a dead brick. Never substitute a different voltage, though — that can finish the job the surge started.

The boot-order angle matters too: after an outage, modem and router race to start, and the router usually loses — it boots before the modem has synced and ends up address-less. If the router does power on with a fresh adapter, restart it once more after the modem is fully online.

For the future: modem and router are exactly the devices that earn a small battery backup (UPS). Not to surf through a blackout — to ride out the one-second flickers that corrupt boots and kill adapters. Ten minutes of battery is plenty for equipment whose worst enemy is the flicker, not the long outage.
My cable modem is connected through a splitter in the attic that also feeds two TVs. A neighbor said splitters 'eat signal.' Is that real, and does it matter?

It's real physics with real numbers. Every splitter divides the signal power among its outputs. A two-way splitter costs each leg about 3.5 dB — a little more than half the power — and a four-way costs about 7 dB per leg. Splitters daisy-chained in series multiply the loss. Cable modems work within a window of acceptable signal levels; push the incoming level low enough and the modem starts producing errors, renegotiating, and dropping sync — often at busy or hot times of day, which makes it look random.

The attic splitter also ages: connectors corrode, and a splitter rated for old TV frequencies may roll off the higher frequencies modern cable internet uses.

The owner-level fixes are simple. If you can, give the modem the first and cleanest split — a two-way at the entry point, one leg to the modem, one leg to everything else — rather than the end of a chain. Make sure every connector is finger-tight plus a snug quarter-turn, and that the splitter is rated to at least 1 GHz. Beyond that, stop: the signal levels themselves are the provider's to measure and balance. If the modem still won't hold sync on a clean single split, that's your evidence for the call — 'modem on a dedicated first split, still losing sync' closes their favorite line of questioning.
We just got fiber. There's a new box on the wall where the fiber comes in, plus my old router. And something keeps beeping in the closet. What are all these pieces?

The new box is an ONT — an optical network terminal. It's the fiber equivalent of a modem: it converts light pulses on the fiber strand into the Ethernet your router understands. The fiber itself runs from that box out to the provider's network; everything on their side of the ONT is theirs, and the glass strand is fragile — never bend its cable sharply or try to clean its connector.

The beeping is almost certainly the ONT's battery backup. Fiber lines don't carry power the way old phone lines did, so ONTs ship with a battery unit that keeps service (especially phone) alive during outages. A beep usually means the battery is exhausted, failing, or has been unplugged — silencing instructions and the battery's status light are on the unit, and a worn-out battery is the provider's to replace if it's their equipment.

Your old router still does its whole job — Wi-Fi, addresses, firewall — plugged into the ONT's Ethernet port instead of a cable modem. One practical consequence: in a power outage your router needs power too, so if staying online matters, both boxes belong on the same small battery backup. And when you call support, name the pieces correctly — 'the ONT's optical light is red' gets you a very different response than 'the modem box is broken.'
Our smart TV says it's connected to the network, but every app fails to load. The phones work fine. The TV worked until last week. What changed?

When one device fails while the house works, interrogate the device's own choices — starting with which network it joined. Modern routers often broadcast more than one: your main network, a guest network, maybe a separate 2.4 GHz name, maybe an old extender. TVs remember networks, and after a router restart, a TV software update, or a neighborly 'fix,' a TV can rejoin the wrong one — classically the guest network, which is deliberately walled off from the internet path or from the services the apps expect, or a dead extender name that still answers but leads nowhere.

Open the TV's network settings and read, don't assume: which network name is it on, and what address did it get? Forget that network entirely and rejoin your main one, entering the passphrase fresh. While you're there, restart the TV properly — unplug it for thirty seconds; the remote's power button is only standby, and the network stack may not have truly restarted in months.

If it still fails on the correct network while phones thrive, test the TV wired or moved temporarily near the router. Working there convicts its weak radio and the distance. Failing everywhere, with the right network and a real restart, finally convicts the TV itself — and you've proven it instead of guessing it.
Everything in the house is fast except my laptop, which crawls even sitting next to the router. Is the router discriminating against it?

Routers don't hold grudges; laptops accumulate causes. Since the house is fast, the separator has already acquitted the internet and the router's general health. The fault is inside this one machine or its specific link, so work inward from the link.

First, which band is it on? Sitting next to the router, it should be on 5 GHz; if it's clinging to 2.4 GHz — because it saved that network first, or the band steering failed — it'll be slow next to the router and, perversely, was probably fine across the house. Forget both networks and rejoin. Second, the wired test on this machine: plug it in. Fast wired plus slow wireless on a healthy network points at the laptop's own Wi-Fi adapter or its driver — an update, especially after an operating-system upgrade, is the usual fix. Third, look at what the laptop is doing: a cloud backup or photo sync saturating the upload will make everything feel broken while speed tests still flatter, and a VPN left running routes every packet through a distant detour.

The lesson generalizes: when one device dissents from a working house, believe the house. The majority report is data.
People keep mentioning a 'demarcation line' for internet problems. What is it, and why does it matter whose side a fault is on?

The demarcation point — the demarc — is where the provider's network ends and yours begins. For cable, it's typically the grounding block where their drop cable meets your house wiring; for fiber, it's the ONT. Everything beyond it — poles, pedestals, amplifiers, the drop to your house — is theirs: their equipment, their legal responsibility, their repair bill. Everything inside it — your inside wiring, your modem if you own it, your router, your devices — is yours.

It matters for three reasons. Money: a fault on their side is fixed free; a fault on your side may be billed as a service visit, and many providers sell a small monthly 'inside wiring' plan precisely for that boundary. Safety and permission: you should never open a pedestal, work on a pole, or service their amplifier — not your equipment, and some of it carries hazards you can't see. And strategy: the whole point of your home troubleshooting is to arrive at the call with the fault already localized to a side. 'Slow everywhere' gets you a script. 'Ninety-four megabits wired at the modem on a five-hundred plan, modem resynced, one device or all devices the same' gets you a line check and a technician.

You don't fix their side. You prove it's their side. That's the owner's real job.
Our internet drops for a minute or two at random times — sometimes days apart. Restarting always 'fixes' it. How do I ever pin down something this slippery?

Intermittent faults aren't caught by better guessing; they're caught by records. Restarting feels like fixing, but if the drop had already ended — most do, on their own — the restart just took the credit. Stop collecting restarts and start collecting data.

Keep a log where the router lives: date, time, how long, what the modem lights did during the drop, and what the house was doing. Three patterns solve most cases once written down. Drops at the same times daily suggest a scheduled thing — a neighbor's equipment, a provider maintenance window, heat building in an attic splitter by afternoon. Drops correlated with weather point outside, to water or expansion in their plant. Drops when a specific appliance runs point at electrical noise or a dying power supply in your own gear.

Add one objective witness: many routers keep an uptime counter and a log of their own. If the router's uptime resets at each drop, the router is rebooting — its power supply or its firmware. If uptime is continuous but the modem's sync drops, the line is the suspect. Two weeks of this turns 'it just drops sometimes' into a pattern a technician can act on — and often the pattern names the culprit before anyone visits.
My plan says 'up to 500 Mbps.' Wired at the modem I get 470-485 every time. Am I being shorted 20 megabits?

No — you're seeing the plan working as specified, and the 'up to' is doing honest work once you know what it covers. The advertised number describes the capacity provisioned to your modem, not a guaranteed throughput to a test server. Between the two sit real costs: the framing and error-correction overhead of the connection itself, the test server's own load and distance, and your equipment. A wired result consistently at 94–97% of the headline is a healthy line, not a shortfall.

What would actually indict the service: results that swing wildly between runs, a wired-at-the-modem number under about 80% of the tier at quiet hours, or a sharp drop at the same time every evening (that's congestion, a different fault). Consistency is the signature of health — your three runs agreeing within a few percent is the modem telling you the pipe is what was sold.

Keep that 470–485 figure written down. It's your reference number: the speed the house demonstrably can receive. Every future speed complaint gets compared against it, and any test taken over Wi-Fi, in another room, or through three gadgets has to explain its gap against this baseline — not against the number on the bill.
I pay for 500 Mbps. Standing in the kitchen, my phone's speed test says 90. Is my provider lying to me?

Your provider may be innocent and your test is definitely guilty — of measuring the wrong thing. That 90 Mbps is the speed of the whole chain: provider to modem, modem to router, router through two walls and a refrigerator's worth of kitchen to a phone, on whatever band the phone happened to choose. A chain reports its weakest link, and in a kitchen that link is almost never the provider.

The honest test removes links until only the provider remains: laptop, Ethernet cable, straight into the router — better, straight into the modem after a restart — then test. If that number is near your plan, the provider is delivering and your 90 was the price of distance, walls, and the 2.4 GHz band your phone likely grabbed.

This isn't pedantry. People upgrade plans, file complaints, and buy new routers because a kitchen test said 90. If the wired reference is 480, none of those purchases fix the kitchen — placement or a wired access point does. Measure the service at the door before blaming the delivery, then measure the room separately and fix the room.
My router offers two networks, one ending in 2.4 and one in 5. The 5 one is faster up close but dies in the backyard. Why the trade?

Because physics prices frequency. The 2.4 GHz band's longer waves bend around obstacles better, lose less energy passing through walls, and carry farther — but the band is narrow, so there's less room: real-world speeds are lower, and it's crowded with neighbors, Bluetooth, and microwave ovens. The 5 GHz band offers far wider channels and much higher speeds, but its shorter waves are absorbed more by every wall, door, and human body in the path. Same house, two different bargains.

So the bands aren't 'slow network' and 'fast network' — they're 'far network' and 'fast network,' and the right choice depends on where the device sits and what it does. The TV two rooms away streaming video wants 5 GHz if it can hold it. The smart plug in the garage, sipping data, belongs on 2.4, which is also why many smart-home devices only speak 2.4 at all.

Many routers merge both under one name and steer devices between them. That works until it doesn't — a device clinging to the wrong band is a classic cause of 'slow in one room.' When a specific device misbehaves, checking which band it's on is a thirty-second diagnosis.
Two speed test sites give me totally different numbers, and even the same site changes when I pick a different server. Which one is lying?

Neither — they're answering different questions. A speed test measures the path between you and that specific server, right now. A server inside your provider's own network measures the short, pampered path: your line at its best. A server across the country measures your line plus the open internet's congestion, distance, and handoffs between networks — every one of which can bottleneck below your line's capacity.

Distance alone bends results: throughput over a single connection suffers as latency rises, so a far server can cap a healthy gigabit line at a few hundred megabits. Multi-connection tests hide this by opening parallel streams; single-stream tests expose it. That's why the same line can score 900 on one test and 350 on another an hour later, both honestly.

Use each for what it's good for. The near, on-network server is your reference: it answers 'is my provider delivering my tier?' — the question your bill raises. Distant servers answer 'what will real downloads from far away feel like?' — interesting, but not evidence against your line. When you report a problem, report the near-server, wired number. It's the one the provider can be held to.
Every evening around 7 to 10, our speeds fall off a cliff. Mornings are perfect. The provider swears our line tests fine — during the day, of course.

Believe both observations; they're describing a shared pipe at different loads. Cable internet is a neighborhood medium: the coax plant feeds a node serving anywhere from dozens to a few hundred homes, and the capacity of that node is shared. At 8 am, you have it nearly to yourself. At 8 pm, every house on the node is streaming, gaming, and backing up at once, and the shared segment saturates. Your line is fine; the commons are full.

Fiber to the home suffers far less, because each home gets its own strand to a splitter with much more headroom — which is why this complaint is a cable classic.

Your counter-move is documentation, because a daytime line test will always acquit them. Run wired tests at the modem at fixed times — say 10 am and 8:30 pm — for several days, and log the numbers. A clean pattern (full tier at 10 am, a third of it at 8:30 pm, repeatedly) is a congestion case, and the fix is on their side: a node split, which only happens when enough documented complaints accumulate. Say the words 'evening node congestion' and attach the log. You're not asking them to find a fault in your house; you're presenting evidence about their plant, in the only hours it misbehaves.
I bought 'gigabit internet' but my upload speed is only 35 Mbps. Downloads are 940. Is the upload broken?

Not broken — asymmetric by design, and the fine print knew. Most cable plans are built heavily lopsided: something like 1000 down / 35–50 up is a standard cable gigabit tier. The technology divvies the cable spectrum unevenly because households historically consumed far more than they sent, and the advertising leads with the download number because it's the big one.

Whether 35 up is enough depends on what leaves your house. Video calls send a few megabits each; two or three at once is fine. Where it bites: uploading large files, cloud backups that saturate the pipe for hours (and, by filling the upload queue, can make everything else feel laggy), a home business sending video, or a house full of security cameras streaming out.

Fiber plans are usually symmetric — 500/500, 1000/1000 — because the technology doesn't force the trade. If upload is your pain, that's the comparison to shop, or ask your cable provider about business tiers, which often carry fatter upload. But nothing is malfunctioning: your test result is the tier, working exactly as provisioned. The lesson is to read plans as two numbers, and buy the smaller one deliberately.
Speed tests say 600 Mbps, but my video calls still freeze and pixelate. How can both be true?

Easily — because a speed test and a video call measure different virtues. The test measures bulk throughput: how much data per second on a wide-open pipe, usually with several parallel streams, averaged over seconds. A video call needs almost no throughput — two to four megabits — but it needs each packet to arrive promptly and in rhythm. The virtues it starves without are low latency (delay) and low jitter (variation in delay).

A call freezes when packets arrive late or bunched, even on a fat pipe. Culprits: Wi-Fi retransmissions in a noisy room (the test's parallel streams bulldoze through; the call's single delicate stream can't), a saturated upload — someone's cloud backup filling the queue ahead of your voice — or a far-away congested path.

Diagnose in that order. Move the call to a wired connection or nearer the router for one meeting: if it heals, it was the wireless leg. Check what's uploading during calls. Run a test that reports latency under load, not just speed. And tell support the right symptom: '600 down on tests, but latency spikes during calls' points at jitter and bufferbloat. 'My internet is slow' points at a shrug.
I upgraded to a gigabit plan. Downloads wired into the router now cap at exactly 94 Mbps, every single time. Suspiciously exact. What's the ceiling?

That exactness is the confession: 94 Mbps is the practical throughput of a 100 Mbps Ethernet link — Fast Ethernet — after overhead. Somewhere between your router and that computer, a link is negotiating at 100 instead of 1000, and a digital ceiling like that is absolute, which is why every run lands on the same number.

Suspects, in order. The cable: an old Cat5 cable, or a newer one with a damaged pair — gigabit needs all four pairs intact; a cable that lost one pair falls back to 100 and works 'fine,' just capped. The port: something plugged into an old switch, a powerline adapter, or a media converter that's only 100-rated. The device: an older laptop, dock, or USB adapter whose port is Fast Ethernet. Check the link speed where the cable lands — most systems report the negotiated rate (1000/100/10) in network settings, and router admin pages often show it per port.

Swap one element at a time: different cable first (it's the most common and cheapest), different port, different device. The fix is almost never the provider and never the plan. A gigabit service delivered over a 100-megabit straw is 94 Mbps forever, until somebody finds the straw.
When I turn my VPN on, my speed drops from 500 to about 180. Is the VPN company throttling me, or is this just how it works?

Mostly, that's just how it works — a VPN is a detour with overhead, and you're measuring both. Your traffic now travels from you to the VPN server (possibly in another state or country), gets decrypted and re-encrypted, then continues to its destination and back. The encryption itself costs processing — on an older router running the VPN, the little CPU in the box often caps out well below line speed, which is why VPN-on-router is slower than VPN-on-laptop. The detour adds latency and one more network that can congest at peak hours.

180 from 500 is a plausible honest result, especially through a distant or busy endpoint. What you can tune: choose the nearest server location — geography is destiny for VPN speed; try the modern protocols (WireGuard is notably lighter than OpenVPN) if offered; run the VPN on the device rather than the router if the router is old.

What would suggest real trouble: speeds collapsing to single digits, or a VPN that's fast at 3 am and unusable at 8 pm — that's an oversold endpoint; change locations or providers. But a one-half to two-thirds haircut for wrapping your traffic in a tunnel is the physics of the thing, not a conspiracy.
One desktop in our house tests at 40 Mbps wired while everything else gets 450. Same router, same cables as far as I can tell. Where's its missing speed?

If the house is fast and one wired machine is slow, the missing speed is inside that machine or its last meter of cable. Work the short list in order of likelihood.

The link rate: check what speed that port negotiated — a damaged cable or a tired port can drop it to 100 or even 10 Mbps, and the test then reports the straw, not the service. Try a different cable and a different router port; this fixes more cases than everything else combined. The software load: a cloud drive mid-sync, a game launcher downloading in the background, or a backup running will happily eat 90% of a connection while the speed test fights for the rest — test with those paused. The network adapter's driver: after an operating system update, a generic driver can replace the tuned one and quietly cap performance; the machine maker's driver is the fix. And the machine's own ceiling: an old spinning hard drive or a pegged CPU can fail to receive at full speed even when the wire offers it.

The discipline is the separator again: the router has been acquitted by every other device. Don't reboot the house for one citizen.
My speed tests are great, but the moment anyone uploads photos or a big file, everyone's games lag horribly until the upload finishes. The pipe is 500 down, 30 up. Explain this curse.

This is bufferbloat, and your numbers name the trigger: the skinny 30 Mbps upload. When an upload saturates that narrow pipe, packets queue up in an oversized buffer inside the modem or router, waiting their turn. The queue can hold seconds' worth of data. Your game packets — tiny, urgent — arrive at the back of that line and wait behind photo chunks. Throughput is fine; delay explodes from 15 milliseconds to 800. Games and calls don't die from slowness; they die from waiting.

Speed tests miss it because they measure the pipe wide open, not the queue under load; some newer tests report 'latency under load' precisely to expose this.

Fixes, in order of leverage. Enable SQM — Smart Queue Management, often labeled QoS or 'bufferbloat fix' — on the router if it offers it (fq_codel or CAKE are the good algorithms); it manages the queue fairly so urgent packets never wait behind bulk. Set its limits to about 90–95% of your true rates (so, near 450/27) so the queue forms in your smart router instead of the dumb modem buffer. If your router lacks SQM, cap the offending app's upload rate in its own settings. Or schedule the big syncs for overnight.

Notice the diagnosis pattern: the symptom appeared under a specific load, at a specific bottleneck, invisible to the standard test. Matching the test to the symptom is the whole craft.
My friend on fiber brags that his ping is 4 ms and mine on cable is 18 ms. Is that a real difference or marketing?

Real, small, and mostly irrelevant — in that order. Latency is travel time, and the technologies genuinely differ. Cable (DOCSIS) adds delay in how it schedules your transmissions upstream — your modem requests slots and waits to be granted them — worth roughly 10–20 ms to a nearby server. Fiber (PON) scheduling is tighter, and a local test server on fiber often answers in 2–6 ms. Distance then dominates for everyone: light in glass covers roughly 200 km per millisecond, so a server across the country adds 30–40 ms no matter what your last mile is made of.

Does 14 ms matter? For competitive gaming at a high level, marginally — it's part of a total budget that includes the game's servers and your display. For video calls, streaming, browsing, and ordinary gaming, the difference between 4 and 18 is undetectable; those fall apart at 150+, or from jitter — the variation — which is a different fault entirely.

So file your friend's brag under 'true but weightless.' If your connection ever feels laggy, the suspect is almost never the 18 ms baseline; it's spikes — bufferbloat when the upload fills, Wi-Fi retransmissions, a congested evening node. Steady 18 beats jittery 4 every time.
Should I upgrade from 300 Mbps to gigabit? It's $25 more a month. We're two adults, two kids, lots of streaming, and I work from home.

Do the household arithmetic first; it's less flattering to gigabit than the ads. A 4K stream uses roughly 15–25 Mbps. An HD stream, 5–8. A video call, 2–4. Gaming itself downloads little during play — it's latency-sensitive, not bandwidth-hungry; the big downloads are game installs, which are occasional and patient. Your worst realistic evening: two 4K streams (50), one HD stream (8), your video call (4), phones and background noise (10) — about 72 Mbps against your 300. You have fourfold headroom.

Where gigabit genuinely earns: very large households, several simultaneous 4K streams plus heavy downloads, people who regularly pull down 100 GB game installs and value the minutes saved, and — the honest sleeper reason — cable gigabit tiers carry more upload (often 35–50 vs 10–20), which a work-from-home uploader or camera-heavy house may actually feel.

Where it earns nothing: Wi-Fi in the back bedroom. If your pain is a stuttering TV or a dead-zone office, gigabit feeds the same weak wireless leg faster at the router and changes nothing at the chair. Spend the $25 on placement or a wired access point. Upgrade the pipe when the pipe is measurably the constraint — wired tests at peak hours near your ceiling — not when the brochure says bigger.
How do I tell whether my router itself is the bottleneck, separate from the internet service?

Give the router nothing to hide behind: test on both sides of it. Run a wired speed test through the router and write it down. Then connect the laptop directly to the modem (restart the modem so it accepts the new partner), run the same test to the same server, and compare.

If the modem-direct number is much higher, the router is convicted — but ask which of its limits you've hit. Old routers cap out in surprising places: a router from the Fast Ethernet era has 100 Mbps ports no matter what the Wi-Fi logo says; a budget router's processor may top out at 200–300 Mbps of routed traffic even with gigabit ports; and features like VPN, parental filtering, or traffic inspection on an underpowered box can halve throughput when enabled. Test with those off to see the tax.

If both numbers are equally low, the router is acquitted and the fault is the modem or the line. If both are high but Wi-Fi is slow, the router's routing is fine and only its radios or placement are guilty — a different fix entirely.

This two-test pattern is worth the ten minutes every time, because 'new router' and 'provider ticket' are opposite purchases, and this is the cheapest way to know which one you're actually shopping for.
Our router sits in the basement corner where the cable comes in, behind the furnace. Half the house barely gets signal. Is placement really that big a deal?

It's the biggest free deal in home networking. Wi-Fi is a radio broadcast from a point, weakening with distance and taxed by every obstacle. Your router is currently shouting from the worst seat in the house: a corner (half its signal aimed at the yard and the soil), the lowest floor (the upstairs signal must climb through the floor and everything in it), and behind a furnace — a giant metal box that blocks and reflects radio waves.

The placement rules are all geometry. Central beats corner: the middle of the home halves the maximum distance to any room. High beats low: on a shelf or wall-mounted, above the furniture that absorbs signal. Out in the open beats enclosed: not in a cabinet, not behind the TV, not inside a metal rack. And away from big metal and water: furnaces, ductwork, refrigerators, aquariums, and water heaters are all signal-eaters.

The constraint is the cable entry point — but the modem can stay in the basement. A single Ethernet run from the modem to a router placed centrally upstairs is one cable solving the whole map, and it's the standard professional answer. Before buying anything — extenders, mesh, a bigger plan — move the broadcast point. Most 'bad Wi-Fi houses' are good Wi-Fi in a bad location.
I keep the router inside the TV stand cabinet because it looks tidy, doors closed. My spouse blames the cabinet for our bad streaming. Surely a wooden door can't matter that much?

The door is the least of it — it's what's sharing the cabinet with the router. A TV stand concentrates signal enemies: the television itself is a large slab with a metal back panel, often directly behind or beside the router; soundbars, game consoles, and cable boxes add more metal and more electronics radiating noise; and the closed cabinet traps heat, which ages electronics and can throttle a hard-working router.

Wood alone costs a little signal; wood plus a wall of metal-faced gear costs a lot, and the direction it costs most is usually straight through the TV — toward your couch.

Run the honest experiment before arguing further: open the doors and slide the router out onto the top of the stand for one evening, same everything else. If streaming heals, the cabinet was convicted by evidence, not opinion. The tidy compromise that usually ends the debate: router on top of the stand or on a small wall shelf just above it, antennas vertical, with the cables dressed neatly. Visible-but-tidy beats hidden-and-suffocated, and you'll likely find the lights useful the next time something blinks wrong at midnight.
How do I actually find my home's dead zones instead of just knowing the back room 'feels bad'?

Walk the house with a phone and measure, room by room. What you want is signal strength in dBm — a negative number where closer to zero is stronger. Phones hide it in settings or diagnostics, and free Wi-Fi analyzer apps display it directly. As you move, you're reading the physics of your house in real time.

Learn the scale, because it's logarithmic and unintuitive: −40 dBm is excellent (same room as the router), −55 is good, −65 is workable for most things, −70 is marginal — video calls start to fray — and −80 is effectively dead. Every 10 dB is a tenfold change in power, and a single interior wall typically costs 3–10 dB depending on material; you'll watch the number step down as you cross the house.

Sketch a rough floor plan and write the reading in each room, on each band. The map tells you what to fix: a gradual decline with distance is a placement problem; a cliff at one particular wall names the wall's material as the culprit; a room that's fine on 2.4 GHz but absent on 5 GHz is normal physics, not a fault. Measure before you buy — the map distinguishes 'move the router,' 'add an access point in that room,' and 'that wall defeats radio; run a cable' from each other.
I bought a Wi-Fi extender. The back room now shows full bars, but speeds there are worse than half of what I get near the router. Did I buy a defective one?

Probably not — you bought exactly what an extender is, and the halving is its mechanism, not its defect. A typical single-radio extender does its whole job on one channel: it listens to your router, then re-broadcasts to your device, then listens for the reply, then relays it back. Every packet crosses the air twice on the same channel, taking turns. The channel's capacity is shared between the two hops, so the theoretical best is half — and the extender also has to be placed where it can still hear the router well, meaning it repeats a signal that was already weakened by distance.

Full bars mislead here: your phone is reporting its strong new link to the nearby extender, not the quality of the whole path to the internet.

Extenders have their place — cheap coverage for low-demand corners, a garage sensor, a guest room that browses. For real throughput in a dead zone, the honest upgrades are: a mesh system, whose nodes use a separate radio (or a wired link) for the backhaul conversation; or better, an access point fed by an Ethernet cable, which loses nothing to relaying at all. The rule of thumb: repeating is for reach, wiring is for speed.
Extender, mesh system, or a second access point — everyone recommends a different one. How do I choose without a sales pitch?

Choose by asking how the extra coverage talks back to the router — that's the whole difference. An extender repeats on the same radio and channel: cheapest, roughly halves throughput on that hop, often broadcasts a separate network name your devices must choose between. A mesh system is a coordinated team: nodes hand devices off intelligently under one name, and better kits use a dedicated third radio (or a cable) for node-to-node traffic, so the relay tax mostly disappears; they're the easy, pretty, pricier option. A wired access point is a second broadcast point fed by Ethernet: no relay tax at all, full speed, one name if configured so — the best performance per dollar, at the cost of running a cable.

So the decision tree is honest. Can you get a cable to the dead zone — through a basement, attic, or along a wall? Then an access point wins outright. No cable possible and the dead zone needs real speed (office, TV)? Mesh with a dedicated backhaul radio. Just need the far corner to stop being dead for light use? The extender you already own is fine.

Beware one trap in all three: adding broadcast points to a house whose real problem is interference or a dying router amplifies the problem. Diagnose first — the map from a phone walk tells you whether you're buying reach, speed, or neither.
Wi-Fi is strong everywhere except my home office, which is only 25 feet from the router. The only thing between them is the fireplace. Can one fireplace do that?

Yes — a fireplace is one of the great Wi-Fi walls in a house. What looks like decoration is a masonry chimney: brick or stone, several inches thick, often with a metal flue and a metal damper inside. Masonry attenuates radio heavily, and metal reflects and blocks it. Twenty-five feet through open air is nothing; twenty-five feet through a chimney breast is like another house entirely.

The signature matches your description: fine everywhere, dead in one specific room at short range. Distance-based problems fade gradually; material problems make cliffs, and a signal-strength walk will show the number plunging as you step into the chimney's shadow.

Workarounds respect the physics instead of fighting it. Best: get a broadcast point on the office's side of the chimney — an access point on a cable run that goes around, or a mesh node placed where it can see both the router (around the chimney, not through it) and the office. Moving the main router a few feet sideways sometimes slips the office out of the shadow cone. What won't work: a stronger router shouting louder through brick, or an extender in the office — it would sit in the same shadow, faithfully repeating a whisper. Diagnose the obstacle, then route around it — literally.
Our house has metal ductwork running through the walls and foil-backed insulation from a remodel. The Wi-Fi map looks like Swiss cheese. Is the house itself the problem?

Parts of it, yes. You've named two of the most effective signal blockers used in construction. Metal ductwork is a system of large hollow conductors snaking through walls and ceilings; radio waves reflect off and are absorbed by them, and a duct crossing between router and room can carve a clean dead shadow. Foil-backed insulation is worse in principle: it's a continuous metal film, and a room wrapped in it approaches a Faraday cage — signal gets in mainly through the door opening and windows, like light into a box.

This is why your map is patchy rather than uniformly weak: it's not distance, it's shadows and reflections, room by room, sometimes chair by chair.

The strategy for a radio-hostile house is to stop trying to punch through and instead put the signal inside each space. Broadcast points belong in the rooms or the hallways serving them, fed by cable that doesn't care about foil. One central router will never serve a foil-wrapped floor plan well no matter its price. In genuinely difficult construction, professionals think like electricians: wire the fixed points (offices, TVs), let Wi-Fi serve the mobile and the near. Your house isn't broken; it's just honest about physics, and the fix is architecture, not amplification.
Three different gadgets have failed to fix my far bedroom. A coworker says 'just run a cable.' Is that really the answer, or is he being a purist?

He's being an engineer. Every wireless fix for that bedroom shares one flaw: they all depend on the same weak radio path through the same walls. An Ethernet cable doesn't negotiate with the walls at all. One run — from the router, through a basement or attic or along baseboards, to a small access point or switch in the far end of the house — converts your worst room into a wired neighborhood. Devices there get full speed; the access point broadcasts from inside the dead zone instead of shouting into it from outside.

The numbers forgive a lot: a standard Ethernet run is good for 100 meters (about 328 feet) at full gigabit — far longer than any house needs — and cable and a basic access point together usually cost less than the second mesh kit you were about to buy.

Running it is less forbidding than it sounds: unfinished basements and attics make it an afternoon's fishing job; where that's impossible, flat cable under carpet edges or raceway along a baseboard works, and powerline or coax (MoCA) adapters can borrow existing wiring as a second-best. The purist's real point stands: wireless is for mobility. For a fixed room that has failed three wireless rescues, stop rescuing wirelessly. Pull the cable once; the problem stays solved for a decade.
Two-story house: router on the ground floor, and the upstairs bedrooms directly above it get worse signal than rooms farther away on the same floor. How is directly above worse?

Because most router antennas don't broadcast in a sphere — they broadcast in a donut. A vertical stick antenna radiates strongly outward horizontally and weakly straight up and straight down, along its own axis. Your upstairs bedrooms sit in the donut's hole: near the router in distance, but in the weakest direction of its pattern, with a floor's worth of joists, subfloor, and possibly tile or radiant heating in between.

Same-floor rooms, even farther ones, sit in the fat part of the pattern with only drywall in the way. Distance loses to geometry again.

Fixes follow from the shape. Some routers let you angle one antenna horizontally, which tips a donut to serve the vertical — worth trying, it's free. Better for a two-story house: put the router on the middle floor if there is one, or accept the classic two-point design — router downstairs, one access point upstairs on a cable, each floor served by a pattern aimed at it. Ceiling-mounted access points are designed with a downward-tilted pattern for exactly this reason.

The general lesson: coverage is three-dimensional and directional. When a near room is inexplicably dead, think about the shape of the broadcast, not just the distance to it.
I've turned the detached garage into an office, about 60 feet from the house. Wi-Fi from the house barely reaches. What are my real options?

Sixty feet of open air plus two exterior walls is a lot to ask of a house router, and exterior walls are heavier than interior ones — siding, sheathing, insulation, sometimes foil or stucco's metal lath. Rank your options by reliability. Best is a cable: a direct-burial Ethernet run in a shallow trench or conduit. At 60 feet you're far inside Ethernet's 100-meter limit, and the garage gets house-grade internet permanently; add a small access point there and you're done for a decade. It's a weekend of digging and the last time you'll think about it.

Second: a wireless point-to-point bridge — two small outdoor radios, one on each building, aimed at each other across the clear line of sight. They form a dedicated link that behaves like a cable for a few hundred feet easily; then an access point in the garage serves your devices. This is the standard answer when digging is impossible.

Third, and weakest: a mesh node in the garage window. It must hear the house through both walls and the yard — usually marginal, weather-sensitive, and slow. Powerline adapters depend on the garage's electrical feed and are a lottery. Notice the pattern: every good answer gives the garage its own local broadcast fed by a real link. The bad answer asks the house router to shout farther.
We have a big house — 4,000 square feet, three floors. The ISP's installer said one good router is enough. It isn't. Was he wrong or is my router broken?

He was reciting the brochure. Router range claims are measured in open air, and your house is not open air: it's three floors of joists, ductwork, masonry, and distance. A single broadcast point has a realistic useful radius of a room or two through construction — a few thousand square feet of open-plan space, much less of a subdivided three-story. At 4,000 square feet across floors, one box is not a plan; it's a hope.

Your router probably isn't broken. It's being asked to do geometry it can't. The professional design for your house is unglamorous: a wired backbone with a broadcast point per floor — access points on Ethernet runs, placed centrally on each level, all sharing one network name so devices roam. Mesh systems approximate this and work well in big houses if the nodes can be placed with good links between them (ideally, wire the nodes too — mesh with wired backhaul is just access points with better manners).

Budget-wise, this is a cabling job more than an electronics job. If running cable everywhere is impractical, prioritize: wire the floor with the office and the main TV, let mesh cover the rest. But retire the one-box expectation — no router at any price repeals walls.
My mesh system has one network name, but my phone clings to the far node as I walk around, crawling, until I toggle Wi-Fi off and on. Why won't it just switch?

Because roaming is the client's decision, not the network's — and phones are conservative voters. Your phone chooses when to let go of its current access point, and most clients hold on until the signal is truly dreadful, because switching has a cost: a brief interruption, and the risk of flapping between two points. Standing in the kitchen equidistant from two nodes, your phone may stay loyal to the bedroom node at −78 dBm while a −50 node sits ignored overhead.

Mesh systems help at the margins — they can suggest, and some can actively nudge or briefly refuse a client to encourage a move — but they can't order a stubborn client to roam. Apple and Android devices each have their own thresholds, and older devices are worse.

Practical mitigations: don't over-provision — too many nodes too close together makes every spot a border dispute; space them so each location has one clearly-best answer. If your system offers band steering and roaming-assist settings, enable them. And accept the manual toggle as a legitimate tool for the one sticky laptop that lives on a desk: give that desk a wired connection or a nearby node, and let the phone do what it does. Roaming is a negotiation; you can improve the terms, but the client always signs.
I want to move the router to the middle of the house, but the cable outlet is in the corner bedroom. Am I stuck with the corner?

Not stuck — but understand the two pieces are separable. The modem must live where the provider's line enters (that corner outlet), unless the provider moves the drop. The router, though, can live anywhere an Ethernet cable reaches. The classic layout for your house: modem stays in the corner, a single Ethernet run crosses the house — through the basement ceiling, the attic, or along a wall — and the router sits centrally, broadcasting from the good seat.

Alternatives when a long run is ugly: ask the provider to relocate the entry point; installers do it for a fee, and if you're having other work done it can be worth it. Or keep the modem-router combo in the corner as the gateway and add one wired access point centrally — functionally the same result, with the corner box's Wi-Fi optionally turned off so devices don't cling to it.

What doesn't work: moving the modem to an outlet fed by a chain of splitters and old cable in another room and hoping. The modem's signal quality is set by that wiring, and a pretty location with a starving modem is worse than an ugly corner with a clean feed and a long Ethernet run. Move the broadcast, not necessarily the modem.
My apartment is tiny — 600 square feet — and the router is never more than 20 feet away, yet Wi-Fi is erratic. How can coverage be bad in a shoebox?

Because in an apartment building, your problem isn't reach — it's company. Your 20 feet of air is shared with every neighbor's network above, below, and beside you, all broadcasting in the same two bands. Your devices hear a dozen networks at similar strength and spend their time contending: waiting for airtime, retrying through collisions, dodging interference. Distance is trivially fine; the medium is crowded.

This diagnosis flips the usual fixes. A more powerful router makes the shouting worse — yours and everyone's. Extenders add more transmitters to the same brawl. What helps is escaping contention: use the 5 GHz band wherever possible (more channels, shorter range means fewer neighbors reach you), pick the least-used channel rather than trusting 'auto' blindly, prefer wired connections for the fixed heavy lifters (TV, console, work computer) to subtract them from the air entirely, and place the router away from the shared wall with the neighbor whose network is strongest.

Test the theory in one minute: run a speed test at 3 pm and at 11 pm or early morning. If the shoebox is fast when the building sleeps, your Wi-Fi was never weak — it was outnumbered.
Our baby monitor camera keeps dropping offline. It's in the nursery, one room away from the router. Everything else in the house is fine. Is the camera just junk?

Maybe — but 'one room away' deserves a second look before the verdict, because cameras are the frailest Wi-Fi citizens in a home. They usually speak only 2.4 GHz, with small antennas and low transmit power, and they must sustain an upload stream constantly — the most demanding job on the network — while mounted high in a corner, often the worst seat in the room. 'One room away' through a wall with a closet full of clothes and a metal-framed mirror can be a genuinely hard path.

Do the cheap tests in order. Stand in the nursery doorway with your phone and read the 2.4 GHz signal strength; if it's weaker than about −70 dBm at the camera's spot, the camera is being asked to work in a hole. Move the router even a few feet — out from behind the TV, up onto a shelf — and retest; small moves make big differences at the margin. Check whether the camera is dropping at particular times (microwave hours, evening congestion) which points at interference rather than reach.

If the signal is decent and it still drops, suspect the camera's power supply (a sagging adapter causes exactly this flakiness) or the camera itself. But convict the location first: most 'junk cameras' are mediocre radios in bad seats, and a three-meter router move is a cheaper fix than a return label.
The router used to sit on a shelf. I moved it behind the big aquarium during a tidy-up, and the living room Wi-Fi fell apart. My family says it's the fish tank. That's not real, is it?

It's real, and your family wins this one. Water is an excellent absorber of Wi-Fi frequencies — 2.4 and 5 GHz are both strongly attenuated by it, which is related to why microwave ovens, working near 2.45 GHz, heat food's water so effectively. A large aquarium is a wall of water: fifty-plus gallons between your router and the living room will eat most of the signal trying to pass through, and the glass and the water's surface reflect and scatter the rest.

It's the same reason signal dives behind water heaters, through bathrooms full of plumbing, and even through a crowd of people at a party — bodies are mostly water too.

Move the router back out — beside the tank is fine, behind it is a shadow. You'll likely recover the room entirely, because nothing else changed. File the principle for the next tidy-up: Wi-Fi wants line-of-sight-ish paths through air and light materials. Metal blocks it, masonry taxes it, and water swallows it. Arrange the shelf accordingly.
My phone's Wi-Fi list shows about forty networks. My connection stutters every evening even though my own signal is strong. What am I looking at?

A crowd, all sharing a few lanes of air. Your strong signal means your router's voice reaches you clearly — but Wi-Fi devices take turns speaking on a channel, and every network on your channel, plus the overlapping ones, is part of the queue. Forty visible networks means your airtime is being divided with the whole building, and evenings are when everyone spends it: streaming, calls, backups. Your packets wait, collide, and retry — that's the stutter, and no signal-strength bar displays it.

The survey is your diagnostic tool. A Wi-Fi analyzer app will show which channels are occupied and how strongly. On 2.4 GHz there are really only three usable lanes (1, 6, 11); on 5 GHz there are many more, and its shorter range means fewer neighbors intrude. Moving your busy devices to 5 GHz and choosing the emptiest channel available is often a dramatic fix in a dense building.

Also subtract yourself from the fight where you can: every fixed device you wire — TV, console, desktop — stops competing for air. In a forty-network building, the best Wi-Fi strategy is partly not using Wi-Fi.
People say on 2.4 GHz you should only use channels 1, 6, or 11. Why those three, and what's wrong with, say, channel 3?

Because 2.4 GHz channels overlap like shingles. The band is divided into channels numbered 1 through 11 (in North America), but each Wi-Fi transmission is about 20 MHz wide while the channel centers sit only 5 MHz apart. A network on channel 1 actually occupies the spectrum of channels roughly 1 through 3; channel 6 occupies 4 through 8's territory; 11 sits clear above. Channels 1, 6, and 11 are the only trio that don't step on each other at all.

Here's the counterintuitive part: sharing channel 6 exactly with a neighbor is better than sitting on channel 8 next to them. Networks on the same channel can hear each other and politely take turns — the protocols coordinate. Networks on partially overlapping channels can't decode each other; they just hear noise, transmit over each other, collide, and retry. Partial overlap is ruder than honest sharing.

So the rule is: pick 1, 6, or 11 — whichever has the weakest competing signals — and never the in-between numbers, however empty they look on a list. The analyzer graph, which draws each network as a wide hump rather than a point, makes this instantly visible. You're not choosing a number; you're choosing a stretch of spectrum.
My router brags about 160 MHz channels on 5 GHz. My neighbor says in our apartment building I should set it to 20 or 40 MHz instead. Who's right?

Your neighbor, most likely — and the reasoning is the speed-versus-share trade. A channel's width is how much spectrum each transmission grabs. Wider means faster peak speeds for you, in clear air. But a 160 MHz channel swallows most of the usable 5 GHz band at once: it overlaps every neighbor, forces your network to contend with all of them, and — critically — wide transmissions are more fragile: if any slice of that wide channel is busy or noisy, the whole transmission waits or retries. In a dense building, a wide channel is a wide target.

Narrower channels invert the bargain: lower peak speed per device, but many more independent lanes, so you can find a quiet one, and each transmission is likelier to get through cleanly. Real-world throughput in a crowded building is often higher at 40 MHz on a clear lane than at 160 MHz in a brawl — and latency is steadier, which is what calls and games feel.

In a detached house with distant neighbors, wide channels are free speed; take them. The setting isn't a quality dial, it's a bet on how empty your air is. Read your environment — a two-minute analyzer survey tells you which bet your building rewards — and size the channel to the neighborhood, not the brochure.
Every day at lunch, when someone runs the microwave, the Wi-Fi in the kitchen dies for two minutes. The microwave is brand new and works fine. Is it leaking radiation?

It's leaking a little radio energy — not a health hazard, but a Wi-Fi disaster, and the frequencies explain why. Microwave ovens heat food at about 2.45 GHz, which sits directly inside the 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi band. Ovens are shielded, and the leakage permitted is tiny in health terms — but Wi-Fi signals are fantastically faint, billions of times weaker than the oven's internal energy, so even a whisper of leakage, from a door seal or vent, shouts over every network in the room. Two minutes of popcorn, two minutes of a jammed band.

Note the signature: only 2.4 GHz devices suffer; the 5 GHz band is untouched. So the fixes are about routing around the oven's schedule and spectrum. Move the affected device to 5 GHz if it can. Move the router (or the device) a few meters — leakage falls fast with distance. And don't put the router on top of the microwave or on the same counter stretch, a surprisingly common arrangement.

If the oven jams Wi-Fi from across a large room or through walls, that suggests more leakage than a healthy seal should allow — worth checking the door's fit and cleanliness, and retiring an oven whose door is damaged. But the ordinary case is just physics sharing a band: the oven was there first, at 2.45 GHz, and Wi-Fi moved in next door.
Our wireless baby monitor isn't Wi-Fi, but ever since we set it up, the 2.4 GHz network has been flaky in that half of the house. Can a non-Wi-Fi gadget break Wi-Fi?

Yes — because Wi-Fi's politeness only extends to its own kind. Wi-Fi devices share the band by listening before speaking and taking turns. Many non-Wi-Fi radios — older baby monitors, wireless cameras, video senders, some cordless phones — transmit on the same 2.4 GHz spectrum but don't speak Wi-Fi's etiquette at all. A video monitor is the worst tenant: it may transmit continuously, a constant shout that Wi-Fi devices hear only as noise, backing off and retrying around it. Your network isn't broken; it's being talked over by something that never pauses.

The evidence fits: flakiness localized to that half of the house, starting with the monitor's arrival, hitting 2.4 GHz while 5 GHz stays clean.

Your moves: change your 2.4 GHz channel to 1, 6, or 11 — whichever is farthest from the monitor's frequency (some monitors let you change their channel too; moving the gadget is as good as moving the network). Increase distance between the monitor's camera unit and the router. And where possible, migrate your real devices to 5 GHz and leave 2.4 to the monitor and the smart plugs. You can't teach the monitor manners, but you can choose which room of the spectrum your conversation happens in.
My Bluetooth headphones crackle and drop when I sit near the router, but they're fine across the room. Bluetooth and Wi-Fi are different things — why are they fighting?

They're different protocols sharing one band. Bluetooth also lives at 2.4 GHz. It's designed for exactly this coexistence: it hops rapidly among 79 small channels, hundreds of times a second, and modern Bluetooth listens and avoids the frequencies your Wi-Fi is using (adaptive frequency hopping). Across the room, that dance works fine.

Sitting beside the router breaks the dance for a physical reason: proximity. Your router's Wi-Fi transmissions arrive at your headphones enormously strong at arm's length — so strong they can swamp the headphone's receiver across a wide swath of spectrum, leaving too few clean channels to hop to. The Bluetooth signal from your phone in your pocket, by contrast, is milliwatt-faint. It's not interference as an argument; it's one voice shouting next to your ear while another whispers.

Fixes are geometric and simple. Move your seat or the router a meter or two — the effect collapses with distance. Put the devices you stream from on 5 GHz Wi-Fi, which empties the 2.4 band around you. And if your router lets you reduce 2.4 GHz transmit power in a small home, that can help everything nearby. Different systems, same air: coexistence works until one transmitter gets too close to the other's listener.
My router is set to 'Auto' channel. A forum says auto is garbage and I should pick channels manually. Should I?

Auto is neither garbage nor magic; it's a bet about how often conditions change. A router on auto surveys the air at boot (better ones, periodically) and picks what looks emptiest. Its weaknesses: it only knows what it saw at selection time, it may optimize for the router's location rather than your desk's, and some models make lazy choices — famously clustering on channel 6 or picking an overlapping channel on 2.4 GHz.

Manual selection wins when your environment is stable and you've actually surveyed it: an analyzer walk shows a clearly emptiest lane (say, channel 1 with only a weak distant network), and you set it and forget it. Manual loses when the neighborhood churns — new neighbors, a neighbor's own auto router hopping — and your once-perfect channel becomes the crowded one while you're still congratulating yourself.

The honest protocol: survey once, properly, at the worst time (evening). If there's an obviously better lane than what auto chose, set it manually. Then re-survey in a month or when symptoms change. And check what auto picked before overriding — sometimes it's right and the forum is just loud. You're not choosing a philosophy; you're choosing who re-evaluates, and how often. In a stable house, that's you, once. In a dense, shifting building, letting the router re-decide nightly can genuinely be the smarter setting.
Once in a while my 5 GHz network vanishes for about ten minutes, then comes back by itself. The router log mentions 'DFS' and 'radar.' Is the router broken?

It's obeying the law, and the log is confessing it. Much of the 5 GHz band is shared with radar — weather radar, airport systems. Wi-Fi is allowed there only as a polite guest under rules called DFS, Dynamic Frequency Selection: the router must continuously listen for radar pulses, and if it detects them (or something that looks like them), it must abandon the channel immediately and stay off it for a while — typically 30 minutes before it may even re-check — moving your network to another channel. During the switch and the mandated channel-availability check on the new channel, 5 GHz can be absent for minutes.

So a vanishing 5 GHz network that returns on its own, with DFS or radar events in the log, is the system working exactly as regulated. It happens more near airports, coasts, and weather-radar installations.

Your choices: live with it (the events are usually rare), or move your 5 GHz network to a non-DFS channel — the lower band around channels 36–48 or the upper around 149–161, depending on region. Non-DFS channels are more crowded in apartments precisely because everyone flees there, but they never get evicted by radar. You're trading occasional eviction for everyday company. If the drops are monthly, most households prefer the quiet DFS lane and the rare ten-minute gap.
In my living room, my neighbor's network shows stronger signal than my own router, which is in the bedroom. Should I buy a more powerful router to win?

You can't win a power war, and you shouldn't start one. Transmit power is regulated and most routers already broadcast near the legal limit; a 'more powerful' router buys little. Worse, Wi-Fi is a two-way conversation: even if your router could shout across the building, your phone's reply is limited by its own small transmitter and battery. A louder router mostly extends the range at which devices can hear it but can't answer — the worst failure mode, because devices cling to a network they can barely use.

Your neighbor's strength in your living room just means their router is near your shared wall or floor. The counters are positional and spectral, not muscular. Move your router toward the living room side of your home if that's where you live — a few meters of relocation beats any amplifier. Choose the channel (on 5 GHz especially) where their network isn't; strength matters less when you're not sharing a lane. And wire the living room's fixed gear if you can.

Think of it as seating, not volume: you don't out-shout the next table at a restaurant; you move to a quieter corner and speak in a clearer lane. Your network doesn't need to beat theirs — it needs to not be sitting in it.
My 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi got noticeably worse when I plugged a USB 3 hub into my computer, which sits near the router. That can't be related. Can it?

It can, and it's a documented quirk of physics that Intel published a paper about. USB 3 signaling runs at 2.4 gigabaud-class rates whose electrical noise spreads right across the 2.4 GHz band. A poorly shielded USB 3 cable, hub, or external drive radiates that noise like a tiny jammer, and anything within a meter or so — your router, a wireless mouse dongle, a laptop's own Wi-Fi antenna near the port — hears it as a raised noise floor. The band doesn't get a new network; it gets static.

The signature is exactly yours: onset tied to plugging in the device, worst near the machine, affecting 2.4 GHz while 5 GHz stays clean.

Fixes are mechanical. Move the hub and its cables away from the router and from wireless receivers — even half a meter helps, since the noise falls off fast. Use well-shielded, shorter USB cables; the bargain bin ones are the usual emitters. Plug wireless dongles into a short extension cable to lift them out of the noise zone — the classic fix for a dying wireless mouse. Or move your important Wi-Fi to 5 GHz and let the hub hiss into an emptier room.

It's a good reminder that 'interference' includes anything electrical, not just other networks. When a symptom starts the day new hardware arrives, believe the calendar.
Our kitchen laptop loses Wi-Fi every time the microwave runs, but only the kitchen laptop. What's the simplest fix that doesn't involve a new microwave?

Move that laptop to the 5 GHz network. The microwave's leakage lives at about 2.45 GHz — it jams the 2.4 GHz band and physically cannot touch 5 GHz. If your router broadcasts both bands and the laptop can see the 5 GHz network from the kitchen, joining it ends the problem today, for free.

If the laptop keeps rejoining 2.4 GHz (because it saved that name first, or the router merges both bands under one name and steers badly), make the choice stick: 'forget' the 2.4 network on that laptop, or if your router uses a single combined name, look for a band-steering setting — or split the bands into two names so you decide. Kitchens are usually near the heart of the home, so 5 GHz range is rarely the issue there.

Fallbacks if the laptop is old and 2.4-only: distance is the other cure — the leakage fades within a few meters, so a different seat or the router moved out of the kitchen's line helps; and a wired connection for a kitchen desk setup ends it absolutely. But start with the band change. The oven jams one neighborhood of spectrum; your laptop is simply living in it when it could move across town.
I have cameras, smart bulbs, and plugs crowding my network alongside laptops and phones. Someone suggested putting all the gadgets on 2.4 GHz and keeping 5 GHz for 'real' devices. Sound advice?

Sound, and it's the standard home segregation for good reasons. Smart-home gadgets are ideal 2.4 GHz citizens: they send tiny amounts of data, they often only have 2.4 radios anyway, and that band's longer reach suits devices tucked in garages, ceilings, and gardens. Your laptops, phones, and TVs are the opposite: hungry for throughput, usually near the router, and 5 GHz gives them wide, emptier lanes. Separating the fleets means the gadgets' chatter never contends with your video call.

There's a second dividend: crowding. Every device on a band shares its airtime. Thirty bulbs and plugs gossiping on 2.4 leaves 5 GHz as a clean expressway. And if your router offers a separate IoT or guest network, putting gadgets there adds a security wall as a bonus — more on that in any security conversation.

Two cautions. Your phone must join the gadgets' network temporarily during setup for many devices, then can return to 5 GHz — a common moment of confusion when a bulb 'can't be found.' And a few gadgets misbehave if the phone and the device end up on different networks permanently (local-control features may need same-network access). If a device demands that, it's a candidate for the main network or a return. Otherwise: gadgets on the long-reach band, people on the fast band, and each fleet stops tripping over the other.
Every device in my house has an address like 192.168.1.something. Who hands those out, and what happens if I just unplug things randomly?

Your router hands them out, automatically, through a service called DHCP. When a device joins your network it asks, in effect, 'what's my address, who's the gateway, who translates names for me?' The router leases it an address from its pool — typically something like 192.168.1.2 through 192.168.1.254 — for a set time, commonly 24 hours, and keeps a list of who has what.

The lease system is why unplugging things is mostly harmless: a returning device usually reclaims its old address or quietly takes another. Addresses are rented, not owned, and the router is a patient landlord.

Where this matters for you: the router's list of current leases is the single best census of your network — every device, its name (often), and its address. That's the page to open when you want to know what's connected, find a printer, or spot a stranger. And the lease idea explains a family of mysteries — a device 'disappearing' after an outage often just means it came back wearing a different number, like a hotel guest moved to another room. The front desk — the lease list — always knows.
Our network printer works for weeks, then suddenly nobody can print until I reinstall it. The printer itself seems fine. What's actually breaking?

The printer isn't breaking; its address is moving out from under your computers. The printer gets its address by lease, like everything else. Most of the time it renews the same number and nobody notices. But after a router restart, a long power outage, or the printer sleeping through its renewal window, it may come back with a different address — say .137 instead of .112. Your computers still try to print to the old address, where nothing (or something else) now lives. Reinstalling 'fixes' it because the installer rediscovers the printer at its new address.

The permanent fix is a DHCP reservation: in the router's settings, bind the printer's hardware (MAC) address to a fixed IP, so the router always leases it the same number.
